title: The Rattrap
summary: A poor peddler who sells rattraps believes the whole world is a rattrap that baits people with riches and then catches them. After stealing from a kind crofter and losing himself in the forest, he is taken in at an ironworks, where the trust and compassion of young Edla Willmansson awaken the goodness in him. Selma Lagerlöf’s story shows that kindness can redeem even a hardened man.

notes.heading: About the author
notes.html: Selma Lagerlöf (1858–1940) was a Swedish novelist and the first woman to win the Nobel Prize for Literature (1909). Her stories are marked by idealism, moral insight and the folklore of rural Sweden.

notes.heading: Gist
notes.html: A vagabond peddler survives by selling rattraps and petty theft. He sees the world as a giant rattrap. An old crofter gives him shelter and shows him thirty kronor, which the peddler later steals. Lost in the forest, he realises he himself has been caught in a trap. At the Ramsjö ironworks the ironmaster mistakes him for an old regimental comrade, Captain von Ståhle, and invites him home for Christmas. When the mistake is discovered, the ironmaster wants to throw him out, but his daughter Edla insists on letting him enjoy Christmas. Touched, the peddler leaves behind the stolen money and a rattrap as a gift, signing himself as a captain.

notes.heading: Detailed summary
notes.html:
The rattrap philosophy. The peddler, ragged and hungry, makes rattraps from wire and begs or steals to survive. One day he is struck by the idea that the world, with its lands, seas and towns, is a big rattrap: it offers riches, joys, food and shelter as bait, and those who touch the bait are trapped. The thought gives him bitter pleasure.

The crofter’s hospitality. One dark evening he knocks at a small grey cottage. The old crofter, lonely and without wife or children, welcomes him warmly, serves porridge and tobacco, and plays cards with him. He boasts that his cow brings him thirty kronor and, to prove it, shows the money in a leather pouch hanging from the window frame. The next morning the peddler leaves with him, but later returns, breaks the window and steals the money.

Trapped in the forest. Avoiding the highway for fear of being caught, he wanders into a forest and gets lost. As night falls he realises he has taken the bait and is caught in the rattrap himself. Exhausted, he hears the thud of hammer strokes and finds his way to the Ramsjö ironworks.

The ironworks. The master smith ignores the stranger. The ironmaster, on his nightly round, mistakes the peddler for an old army comrade, Captain von Ståhle, and invites him home. The peddler, fearing the stolen money will be discovered, declines. The ironmaster then sends his daughter Edla, who persuades him with gentle kindness, noticing his fear and assuming he has been in trouble.

Discovery. The next morning, washed, shaved and dressed in good clothes, the peddler is seen in daylight and the ironmaster realises his mistake. He threatens to call the sheriff. The peddler says the world is a rattrap and that the ironmaster too may be caught some day. Edla, however, says he should stay for Christmas, since they had promised him a joyful holiday and he has nowhere to go.

Redemption. The peddler spends Christmas Eve eating and sleeping. On Christmas Day, while the family is at church, they learn that the crofter has been robbed by the peddler. They fear their own silver may be gone. But at home they find a small package left for Edla: a rattrap containing the thirty kronor and a letter. In it he says that because she treated him like a captain, he wanted to act like one, and asks her to return the money to the crofter. He signs as Captain von Ståhle.

notes.heading: Themes
notes.html:
• Materialism as a trap: worldly wealth tempts people and then imprisons them.
  • Redemption through love and trust: Edla’s compassion awakens the peddler’s dormant goodness.
  • Loneliness: the crofter, the peddler and even the ironmaster are lonely; kindness answers this need.
  • Essential goodness of human beings: even the lowest can rise when treated with dignity.

notes.heading: Character sketches
notes.html:
The peddler: poor, cynical and dishonest at first, he views the world as a rattrap. Yet he is not wholly bad; he is thoughtful, witty and capable of shame. Edla’s respect brings out his conscience, and he returns the money.

Edla Willmansson: the ironmaster’s daughter, kind, perceptive and generous. She sees the peddler’s fear and treats him with dignity even after his identity is exposed. She is the moral centre of the story.

The ironmaster: impulsive and proud; quick to welcome and quick to anger, but ultimately respects his daughter’s judgement.

The crofter: lonely, trusting and hospitable; his innocence makes the theft more shameful.

notes.heading: Title justification
notes.html: The rattrap is the central symbol. The peddler sells rattraps, believes the world is a rattrap, falls into one through greed, and finally escapes through Edla’s kindness, leaving a rattrap as a gift. The title thus links his trade, his philosophy and his moral journey.

notes.heading: Message and values
notes.html: Kindness and trust can transform people more effectively than punishment. Greed leads to entrapment, while compassion leads to freedom. Everyone deserves a chance to redeem himself.

keyTerms.definition: A person who travels from place to place selling small goods.
A person who rents and farms a small plot of land; here, the lonely old host.
Swedish currency; the peddler steals thirty kronor.
Owner of the Ramsjö ironworks, Edla’s father.
Food used to lure an animal into a trap; symbol of worldly temptations.
The rattrap stands for the world’s material temptations that ensnare human beings.
Being saved from sin or wrongdoing; the peddler’s moral recovery.

mcqs.q: What thought gave the peddler unexpected pleasure?
options: That he would soon be rich
That the whole world is a rattrap
mcqs.explanation: He enjoyed the bitter idea that the world is a big rattrap, since it had never been kind to him.

mcqs.q: How did the crofter earn his thirty kronor?
options: By selling milk from his cow
mcqs.explanation: The crofter received the money as payment for his cow’s milk, delivered to the creamery.

mcqs.q: Why did the peddler avoid the highway after the theft?
options: He wanted to visit the forest.
He was looking for the ironworks.
mcqs.explanation: Afraid of being caught with the stolen money, he took a forest path and lost his way.

mcqs.q: Whom did the ironmaster mistake the peddler for?
options: Captain von Ståhle, an old regimental comrade
mcqs.explanation: In the dim light of the forge he took him for Nils Olof, Captain von Ståhle, his former comrade.

mcqs.q: Why did the peddler refuse the ironmaster’s first invitation?
options: He feared the stolen money would be discovered.
He wanted to sleep at the forge.
mcqs.explanation: Going to the manor felt like walking into the lion’s den with stolen money in his pocket.

mcqs.q: What made the peddler accept Edla’s invitation?
options: Her threat to call the police
mcqs.explanation: Edla’s kindness and understanding reassured him; she sensed his fear and treated him gently.

mcqs.q: How did the ironmaster discover his mistake?
options: The crofter came to the house.
He saw the peddler clearly in daylight after he was shaved and dressed.
mcqs.explanation: In daylight, washed and shaved, the peddler clearly was not the captain.

mcqs.q: Why did Edla insist that the peddler stay for Christmas?
options: She wanted him to repair the house.
They had promised him Christmas cheer and he had nowhere else to go.
mcqs.explanation: Edla felt it wrong to break a promise of hospitality and turn away a homeless man at Christmas.

mcqs.q: What did the peddler leave for Edla?
options: A rattrap containing the thirty kronor and a letter
mcqs.explanation: He left a small rattrap with the stolen money and a letter asking her to return it to the crofter.

mcqs.q: Why did the peddler sign the letter as Captain von Ståhle?
options: Because he had been treated like a captain, he wanted to behave like one
mcqs.explanation: Edla’s dignified treatment made him rise to the honour of the captain’s name; it marks his moral transformation.

questions.q:
Read the situation and answer: Lost in the forest after the theft, the peddler realises with bitterness that he has been tricked by the very bait he scorned, and that now he too is caught.
(a) What was the ‘bait’ in his case? (1)
(b) Why did he feel caught? (1)
(c) What literary device is the rattrap? (1)
(d) What does this realisation reveal about him? (1)
questions.answerHtml:
(a) The crofter’s thirty kronor.

(b) Fear of being caught had driven him into the forest, where he lost his way and could not get out.

(c) A symbol / extended metaphor.

(d) It shows he has a conscience and can reflect on his own actions.

questions.q: How did the peddler’s view of the world as a rattrap originate?
questions.answerHtml: One day, while thinking about his rattraps, the peddler felt that the world had never been kind to him. He imagined it as a huge trap that offers riches, comfort and food as bait, and once anyone touches the bait, it closes on him.

questions.q: Why was the crofter so talkative and friendly with the peddler?
questions.answerHtml: The crofter was an old man living alone, with no wife or children. He was happy to have someone to talk to in his loneliness. So he shared his food and tobacco, played cards with the peddler and even showed him his savings.

questions.q: What made the peddler finally change his ways?
questions.answerHtml: Edla’s kindness changed him. She treated him with respect even after learning he was a mere peddler and insisted he enjoy Christmas with them. Being trusted like a captain awakened his conscience, so he returned the stolen money and chose to behave honourably.

questions.q: The story focuses on human loneliness and the need to bond with others. Discuss with reference to the characters. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
Lagerlöf’s story shows that loneliness lies beneath many of its characters, and that a human bond can heal it. The peddler wanders alone, rejected and hungry, finding no shelter except grudging charity. His cynicism comes from this isolation.

The old crofter is equally lonely. Without wife or children, he welcomes the stranger with porridge, tobacco and cards, and trusts him enough to show his savings. His warmth comes from a hunger for company.

The ironmaster, a widower whose sons are away, eagerly invites a supposed old comrade home for Christmas, hoping for fellowship. Edla, who keeps her father company, understands this need and extends it to the peddler.

When the peddler is shown genuine human connection and respect, his heart softens. He returns the money and signs as a captain. The story thus suggests that kindness and companionship can rescue people from the trap of loneliness.

questions.q: Compare the ironmaster and his daughter Edla. (120–150 words)
questions.answerHtml:
The ironmaster and Edla differ greatly in temperament and judgement. The ironmaster is impulsive. Seeing a ragged man in the forge, he hastily assumes he is his old comrade, Captain von Ståhle, and insists on taking him home. When daylight reveals the mistake, he becomes angry and threatens to hand the man to the sheriff. His kindness depends on social status.

Edla is gentle, perceptive and compassionate. Even on first meeting, she notices the peddler’s fear and guesses that he may be a thief or an escaped prisoner, yet she treats him kindly. When her father wants to throw him out, she argues that they promised him Christmas cheer and that he should not be sent away on that holy day.

Her goodness is based on humanity, not rank. It is her unconditional respect that transforms the peddler, making her the true moral force of the story.
